results.why: Chrome uniquely resolved the Link header on subresource responses, so a response could downgrade the referrer policy of the request that fetched it and leak the full referrer URL, query string included. Fixed in the 136 line; on a patched build this must be BLOCKED.

results.title: Cross-origin <script src> executes in the embedding origin (XSSI)
results.why: SOP never restricted script *execution* by origin, only reading the source text. A cross-origin script runs with the embedder's authority, so any secret the response body assigns to a global has crossed the boundary. This is the XSSI / JSONP class and it is not a bug in any engine — it is the model working as specified, which is exactly why it remains exploitable.

results.title: window.onerror message sanitisation for cross-origin scripts
results.why: Cross-origin script errors must be reported as the opaque "Script error." with no line or column, otherwise error text becomes a read channel into a cross-origin response body.
results.detail: muted=true msg="Script error."

results.title: sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" escapes its own sandbox
results.why: Granting both tokens to same-origin content is self-defeating: the frame keeps the embedder's origin, so it can reach parent.document, read anything there, and delete its own sandbox attribute. Any site serving attacker-controlled content (uploads, previews, templates) from its own origin under these two tokens has handed that content full origin authority. The HTML spec warns about this explicitly; no engine treats it as a bug, which is why it keeps shipping.

results.title: Sandboxed cross-origin frame stays confined

results.title: document.domain relaxation with Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?0 on both documents
results.why: The decisive test of whether Chrome 115 removed origin relaxation or merely flipped its default. Both documents are served with Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?0 and both assign the same document.domain. If the cross-origin read then succeeds, relaxation is alive and any site still emitting that header keeps a cross-subdomain hole in its own SOP boundary — a materially different security story from "the feature was removed".

results.title: Unilateral document.domain relaxation does not open the boundary
results.why: The control that keeps RELAX-02 honest. Only this side relaxes; the target does not. This must stay BLOCKED — otherwise relaxation would be an attacker-unilateral SOP bypass against any subdomain, which is a categorically more severe bug than a cooperative legacy feature.
results.detail: self.domain=sop-lab.test (relaxed) target=NOT relaxed setterOk crossRead=blocked, mutual opt-in correctly required

results.title: document.domain relaxation on an insecure origin, with no opt-out header
results.why: Origin-Agent-Cluster is only honoured in a secure context. If that is what carries the Chrome 115 default-flip, then plain http origins never received it and keep document.domain relaxation unconditionally — no header, no cooperation from the server, nothing to opt into. That would make the "document.domain was disabled in 115" summary true only of https, which is a materially different claim. Run as the pair to RELAX-01: identical logic, insecure scheme.

results.title: OffscreenCanvas taint propagates back to the placeholder element (CVE-2025-9180)
results.why: The CVE-2025-9180 mechanism, reconstructed from the fix commit rather than from a writeup, because no public POC exists and Mozilla shipped the fix with no in-tree test. OffscreenCanvasDisplayHelper had no write-only member at all, so tainting a canvas inside a Worker after transferControlToOffscreen() left the main-thread toDataURL()/toBlob() readback ungated. What leaks is raw cross-origin pixel data — a full read primitive, not a timing oracle. Affected: Firefox before 142, ESR before 115.27 / 128.14 / 140.2.
